\chapter*{Pronunciation \& Script --- a reference}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Pronunciation \& script (reference)}
\markboth{Pronunciation}{Pronunciation}

A \textbf{reference}, not a chapter — a place to look things up as you go, never a wall to climb first. Chapter 1 (the reading course) teaches you to decode the script from zero, letter by letter, each letter introduced as a word needs it; this page just collects the sound-and-script facts in one spot. Lessons name the sounds they need and link here.

Transliteration note: this curriculum writes Arabic in both the \textbf{script} (\ar{مرحبا}) and a \textbf{Latin transliteration} (\emph{marḥaban}), with a dot under a letter marking the \textquotedblleft{}heavy\textquotedblright{}/emphatic or throaty consonants.

\section*{The script, in one breath}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \textbf{Right to left.} Eyes and writing both go right $\to$ left.
  \item \textbf{Letters connect.} Most letters join to the next, so a letter has up to four shapes (isolated / initial / medial / final). You don't drill these — you re-meet them inside real words.
  \item \textbf{Short vowels are often unwritten.} \emph{a, i, u} are usually diacritics (harakāt) left off in everyday text; long vowels (ā, ī, ū) are written as letters (\ar{ا} \ar{و} \ar{ي}).
\end{itemize}

\section*{Consonants with no English equivalent}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \texttt{ha-heavy} — \textbf{\ar{ح}} (ḥ): a \textquotedblleft{}heavy\textquotedblright{} \emph{h}, breathed hard from deep in the throat (vs. the light \textbf{\ar{ه}} \emph{h}). \emph{marḥaban}, \emph{ṣabāḥ}.
  \item \texttt{kha} — \textbf{\ar{خ}} (kh): a guttural scrape at the back of the throat = Scottish \emph{loch}, German \emph{Bach}, \textbf{Spanish \emph{j}} (\emph{jueves}). \emph{khayr}.
  \item \texttt{ayn} — \textbf{\ar{ع}} (ʿ, \textquotedblleft{}ʿayn\textquotedblright{}): a tightening deep in the throat, voiced. No English equivalent; approximate it. \emph{ʿalaykum}, \emph{ʿafwan}.
  \item \texttt{hamza} — \textbf{\ar{ء}} (ʾ): a \textbf{glottal stop}, the catch in \textquotedblleft{}uh-oh.\textquotedblright{} \emph{masāʾ}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{غ}} (gh): like a French/guttural \emph{r} (gargled \emph{g}). \textbf{\ar{ق}} (q): a \emph{k} made far back, at the uvula.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Emphatic (\textquotedblleft{}heavy\textquotedblright{}) consonants}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \texttt{emphatic-sad} — \textbf{\ar{ص}} (ṣ), \textbf{\ar{ض}} (ḍ), \textbf{\ar{ط}} (ṭ), \textbf{\ar{ظ}} (ẓ): heavier, deeper versions of \emph{s, d, t, dh}, made with the tongue lower and the mouth fuller. They genuinely change the word (\ar{ص} \emph{ṣ} $\neq$ \ar{س} \emph{s}). \emph{ṣabāḥ}.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Light consonants (close to English)}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \texttt{shin} — \textbf{\ar{ش}} (sh) = English \emph{sh} (\emph{shukran}). \textbf{\ar{س}} (s) = plain \emph{s}. \textbf{\ar{ب}} (b), \textbf{\ar{ل}} (l), \textbf{\ar{م}} (m), \textbf{\ar{ر}} (r, a tapped/rolled \emph{r} like Spanish), \textbf{\ar{ن}} (n), \textbf{\ar{ك}} (k), \textbf{\ar{ت}} (t) — all near their English values.
\end{itemize}

\section*{The definite article and \textquotedblleft{}sun/moon letters\textquotedblright{}}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item \texttt{sun-moon} — \textbf{\ar{ال}} (al-, \textquotedblleft{}the\textquotedblright{}) attaches to its noun. Before a \textbf{sun letter} (\ar{ت} \ar{ث} \ar{د} \ar{ذ} \ar{ر} \ar{ز} \ar{س} \ar{ش} \ar{ص} \ar{ض} \ar{ط} \ar{ظ} \ar{ل} \ar{ن}) the \emph{l} assimilates and the letter doubles: \emph{al-salām} $\to$ \textbf{as-salām}, \emph{al-nūr} $\to$ \textbf{an-nūr}. Before a \textbf{moon letter} (the rest, e.g. \ar{خ} \ar{ق} \ar{ك} \ar{ب}) the \emph{l} stays: \textbf{al-khayr}. You can hear the sun-letter rule fossilized in Spanish \emph{azúcar} ($\leftarrow$ \emph{as-sukkar}).
\end{itemize}

\section*{The root system (structure, not pronunciation)}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
\setlength{\itemsep}{0.35em}
  \item Most words are built on a \textbf{three-consonant root} carrying a core meaning, poured into fixed vowel \textbf{patterns}: k-t-b (writing) $\to$ \emph{kitāb} (book), \emph{kātib} (writer), \emph{maktab} (office). Learn a root and a few patterns, and you generate a whole family. See the first lesson.
\end{itemize}
